utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Unexpectedly, Judge Fluegge is still not, for urgent personal reasons, not available. He is unable to continue to hear this case. The expectation still is that it will not last for more than five days. Although we expect that he'll not be able to sit this week, we expect him back the beginning of next week. Judge Moloto and myself have considered whether it would be in the interest of justice to continue to hear this case, and we decided that it is. So, therefore, we'll sit under Rule 15 bis for the remainder of this week, as far as we can oversee now. Is the witness ready to be brought into the courtroom? And is the usher ready to bring him in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour. I did have a thought last night. A few more minutes this morning, if I could. It shouldn't take us long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's a few. You know, "few" is a relative concept. If you would specify, that would even be an appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It shouldn't be more than ten minutes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've used about 50 of my hour and a halfs, so I'll well with -- well under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, as far as the Chamber is concerned. And I see Mr. Lukic is also nodding that there is no objection on his side. Well, it's time to lower the level, the volume of your voice again, Mr. Mladic. If there's anything you want to bring to the attention of this Chamber, Mr. Lukic will certainly assist you in doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Todorovic. Before we continue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. McCloskey has a few more questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This morning, I want to show you a short video and ask you a question or two about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to P1147.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's from our trial video. It's what we believe to be 13 June 1996 in the area of Zepa. We'll see General Mladic at a table with others. And I'll ask you a question or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a portion that was played before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have seen this. It does have subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has subtitles and it has all been verified. Therefore no need to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's in evidence. There's never been an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let's play it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "When we finished with that, we started the operation of capturing Avdo Palic, Major Pecanac, whom I sacrificed and infiltrated, stood out there. I told him: 'Young man, you're going there.' And he says: 'Boss, will we see each other again?' 'We'll see each other young man, and if not fuck you. Go and do your job.' "Slowly, slowly, I know that. I'll tell everything."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we play it one more time without the English translation so that we hear General Mladic, and we're starting at 28.0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to hear General Mladic as well on the English channel, because I take that the witness has heard him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I -- if everyone could hear General Mladic so we get the idea of the tone and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we've stopped at 28.56.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the man with his arms crossed in the centre of this photo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you heard General Mladic and what he had to say. That -- about mentioning Major Pecanac. General Mladic said that in a rather personal way, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a part of his private conversation. A relaxed atmosphere, not a combat task; simple conversation at a table. Obviously they were celebrating something. It was a private exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you a similar --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But it shows a personal connection between Mladic and Pecanac, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. They were officers. They were members of the Main Staff. They socialised. This is somewhere in a meadow. It is the year 1996. They just socialised. This is a private event, as it were. There's nothing out of the ordinary here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we heard Mladic say: "When we finished with that we started the operation of capturing Avdo Palic, Major Pecanac, whom I sacrificed and infiltrated, stood out there." What happened to Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was negotiating the safe exit of the BiH army from Zepa to avoid casualties. They got in touch with him and made a deal for the troops, the wounded, and the civilian population to get out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know that he was held by the VRS and murdered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is possible. I don't know what happened to him. But I know that he was involved in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to one more video on this topic of the relationship between General Mladic and Mr. Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is 01299a. And this is from a video that was retrieved from a search of General Mladic's home in Belgrade. We believe it's in about June of 1997 associated with the celebrations surrounding General Mladic's son and his wedding, Darko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there's really nothing much to hear so there has been no transcript, no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'll not rely on the text, we'll put the volume low.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get the volume up a little bit so that we hear this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you recognise a famous Yugoslav song, the "Dotako sam dno zivota" by Tomo Draskovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a love song about hell in the abyss and sorrow and pain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the interpretation. This is a typical pub song. This is what you sing when you're relaxed, in a bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the man holding General Mladic, singing with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer this clip into evidence and have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number of this clip would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7382, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. I see that it -- that the CD is provided. Mr. Lukic, you announced yesterday that you would need another 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Todorovic, once again, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I won't focus on the video-clips. We have to focus on what was said yesterday in this courtroom. You mentioned The Slovenian and my colleague, Mr. McCloskey, clarified that and established that you meant Franc Kos when you had -- when you said The Slovenian?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 35404, he asked you -- or, rather, Judge Orie asked you whether he was your superior at the moment when Pecanac turned up and you said on line 15 that he was at that moment, indeed. My question is this: Were you in a position to issue orders to The Slovenian?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the hierarchy of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, was Franc Kos actually above you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also on transcript page 35406, lines 16, through page 35408, line 1, you talked about Pecanac, about whether he was the aide-de-camp of General Mladic, whether he was close to him, whether he carried out General Mladic's orders. Were you ever present when General Mladic issued an order to Major Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you see Pecanac with General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Dragasevac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours I would like to clarify some translation. Yesterday at page 35402, line 25, sentry duty was mentioned. Then it was translated on page 35408, line 15, as the same words as officer from the gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I don't know whether we should invite the witness to take his earphones off --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you deal with any matter that -- Mr. Todorovic, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since the witness took his headphones off, he always used the same term and the term is recorded as his previous testimony at page 35410 as "gate-keeper." So it could create some confusion, but I think that every time, actually, this gentleman said "gate-keeper," so if you -- I don't know how we could clarify with him, the English versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's -- one second. You say he always used the same term and the term is recorded in his -- as his previous testimony as "gate-keeper."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you say at least that is how it is translated to us that he actually said "gate-keeper," so that's for me the same. Now, I think if you have any concerns about confusion, then I think the best way of dealing with it is that you use the word he used in his own language, and then you ask him to explain what that word means for him, that he can describe what a gate-keeper's task is or what his duty is and how he performs that duty. I think that's the most appropriate way of clarifying the issue. Witness, "Svedok." Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you mentioned the reception.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was there at the entrance to your base?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The four elderly men working there. They were mobilised. They were gate-keepers. They had to register everybody who entered the barracks, their names, the registration plates of the vehicles. Nobody could enter the compound if they did not report to them. They were gate-keepers. They were soldiers, foot soldiers, but somewhat older than the rest of us. I can give you their names, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go on. Give us the names.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojislav Obrenovic was one of them. Ratko Tomic, Slobo Vasiljevic, Milan Simanic. From time to time, they would be replaced by one of our soldiers from the detachment to relieve one of those people who were constantly on the gate-keeping duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that this is a good enough explanation. At least for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad that I could tell that you none of them were officers, that they were simple gate-keepers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, just to avoid whatever confusion, when you say that one of the gate-keepers, as you called them, was Vojislav Obrenovic, that is not the same person as Zoran Obrenovic. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to be sure that there's no confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to tackle another topic. On page 35415, and also on page 35416 of the transcript, there was a reference made to the women that were in Pelemis; they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those women, were they released at one -- at one moment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those women were supposed to be exchanged for Stanimir Pelemis who had been in charge of that activity. He organised everything. I don't know whether he consulted with Pelemis, whether that was approved or not. I did not have access to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was not clear enough. Do you know -- and if you don't, just tell us so. Do you know if those women left to the site under the control of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Groups passed by. Some were returned to Vlasenica, the others to Batkovic. Miso did not allow them to enter the village because we didn't know then how the line would be maintained, what would happen, and things were done in a haste.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still not a clear answer. First of all, do you have any personal knowledge as to what happened to these women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that one group arrived. I don't know where from. And I personally escorted them to the school and then they went to the BiH army line. I was the one in charge. They all passed. They were not interrogated. Nothing happened to them. A corridor was opened. I escorted them. They still live there today. Some of them I know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, was anything or any person received in exchange for these women leaving for BiH-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there was no exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally let them through. We didn't know what to do with them. We didn't have anything to eat, never mind to keep them too. The line was open. I took them in front of our line and I brought them almost in front of their line. And then when I was coming back, I encountered an ambush set up for me by the B and H army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But yesterday you told us, I think several times, that they were held ready for an exchange; but finally they were not exchanged, if I understand you well, because nothing was received in return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the first group that was brought. Six women and seven, eight, nine, ten men. They were taken back somewhere. I don't know where. I did not take part in that. I know about this group, 100 per cent, that I took through that all of them passed through. As for these others that were taken away, I don't know if they were take back to Vlasenica, Sekovici, I don't know. I went to prepare the assault detachment in Vlasenica to fix up the dormitories, the barracks. I went there from time to time. I don't know what was happening. I was coming and going. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused because we're not talking about two groups, whereas yesterday we were talking only about one group. Now, yesterday you told us that these were the woman who did the laundry and questions were put to you on whether they socialised with young Serb soldiers. Now, was that the group that was held ready for exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm talking about now is the first group of six women and those men, the ones that were doing the laundry. I don't know where they were returned to and to whom. There was no exchange. As and for this other group that I took, I released them in front of our lines between the two lines of front lines. At the line of separation. And not a single hair on their head was harmed. They went through and they're still alive to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you say, talking about that first group, I don't know where they were returned to and to whom. There was no exchange. If you don't know where they went, how could you know that they were not exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't there when I -- they weren't there when I came back there for the second and the third time. I didn't see anybody of them there. I mean, it's a small village. You can see all the houses there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's just a conclusion that because you didn't see them when you dealt with the second group, that it is your conclusion that they were not exchanged, although you have no knowledge as to where they went and how they went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us and can we -- we can go into private session if you think it's necessary. Could you please tell us the names of the people in the group that you took.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people from Vlasenica whom I didn't know but I know where one of the women lives. In Kladanj, in Sigonsko Naselj [phoen], I know a lady very well. I took her to get some papers. She left a daughter. Her name is Jasmina. The little girl was taken care of. She was exchanged. Her name was Irma. She's already a young woman now, the same age as my son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say these were people from Vlasenica, are you talking about the first group, or are you talking about the second group? The group you dealt with personally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second group. Thank God they all passed through. They're all alive. And most of them relocated all over Europe. Some of them even got to the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And earlier you said you knew these people in the group you dealt with personally, and now you say, apart from Irma, you -- no, the transcript is not complete. I have some difficulties in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll continue with the line of questions. Maybe it would clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's my recollection that I heard in the English language, although it doesn't appear on the transcript, the word "exchanged." I don't know whether that's -- but please continue at this time, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Todorovic, was this group exchanged for someone or were they released to go to the other side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I took?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The one that you took.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is being treated differently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slow down. The interpreters have problems in following you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, okay. [Interpretation] Everyone was released, and in our area, we say, well, let's just exchange them without any compensation. I was proud to have done that. I am glad to say that they were all alive. Today, I don't have any comment on that, and you can treat it as if I said it was an exchange or if they were freed. I am not well versed in legal language. I'm just speaking in regular people talk. They were all released safely. All the children are well. There are no consequences for me or for them. Nobody on the Serbian side mistreated them while I was taking them through the village. It all went according to the most proper order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how many people were there in that group that you took through?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were plenty of them. They were not recorded. There was not list or anything like that. They were just brought there up until behind our line to some village, Morica Volikuca [phoen] it's called, and they wanted to release them there, and then it turned out that there was some contacts, and then we provided some trucks, and I took them directly through the line and let them go. They're alive to this very day. Some of them are in Kladanj. I'm from Kladanj. I don't know them individually by name, but I know where they are and who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us this. You said that there were many of them. Were there 10, 50, 100? Can you give us a figure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a bus. As many people that can fit into a bus. There were children there, women, elderly people. I took them all through nicely. I let them go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Irma, this little girl, where was she accommodated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was placed with a family, the family of Jerko Vucinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long did Irma stay in that house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she stayed there. My son was there also, my child. I think maybe for a year. Perhaps less or perhaps longer. Because I wasn't there anymore. I moved to Vlasenica. But I went there to visit my wife and my child from time to time. They were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Jerko Vucinovic, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jerko was just a regular man. He was on the line, he had his own household, and he was captured in one of the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since this was not on the line of questions put to you by the Prosecutor, I'm going to -- well, what did Jerko tell you? Just briefly. Was he released and what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jerko, when he was released, he said that that little girl, who's already a young girl now, had saved him when he -- when she came to Tuzla to visit the prison. She called him uncle and she sat in his lap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr. Todorovic. When you saw these women next to the water, that first group we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in the centre of the village, were they under any guard? Did any armed persons guard them by the water? Were they taken there, did you see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't see or there were no guards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nobody there. There is the centre of the village. There were not enough soldiers to -- to supply the line properly, never mind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, thank you. These are all the questions that we had for you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This group of women was never guarded, Witness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an old man with them. We used to call him Uncle Momir. He was a grandpa. I mean, if he can be considered as a person who guarded them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there only one person who was in such a position which you could consider as being guarding the women?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him there with them. I wasn't there all the time, so I can't really say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yesterday you told us that there were some older geezers that guarded them. So then you were talking in the plural and not -- although you specified one person, you talked about more persons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't be there all the time. There were a couple of grandpas there, a couple of elderly women, a couple of kids of ours of Serbian ethnicity. There were always 20 or 30 people around that water, men, women, children, when there was no shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now are you telling at this moment that when you said there was a couple of grandpas there, there were always 20 or 30 people there - men, women, and children - but the women and the children were not the guards but were then guarded, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably one of the -- of these men had to be there. Look -- to -- to look at them. I mean, to keep an eye on them. There was no need for a lot of guards, ten guards or anything like that. The only danger was from the shelling. I really didn't know anything about it. I couldn't do anything, go up there. I -- this was at a higher level. I am just a -- I was a regular soldier. And I was told to do this or do that. I didn't couldn't constantly spend time there with those people and those men and those women in the village. I had to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, now, there's a suggestion in your answer, and I give you an opportunity to comment on that, that these women were guarded in order to protect them against shelling. I don't know how that works, but if you have any explanation for that, or if you didn't suggest that, but that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that -- I said that there would always be 20 or 30 men there, women, elderly men, and there was no other danger for them there other than shelling, and that there was a man there who kept an eye on them so that they could be taken into the house where they were accommodated. I mean, nobody can save you from a shell. I know very well what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you introduced spontaneously yesterday the word "guarded," isn't it? Not specifically asked about whether they were guarded. The question about whether they socialised, and then you came up with that they were guarded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to say that that man who was with them, that Momir, I couldn't call him a shepherd. I had to call him a guard, security. I can't call him a shepherd. These are not sheep. These are people. These were women that he was keeping an eye on. Well, we can put it like that, that he was keeping an eye on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to take some -- a brief moment to clear up some of the Pelemisi issues that have been raised here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, what happened to the 16-year-old Muslim girl that was held at Pelemisi? Her name is Ferida Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the field with soldiers also. And when I came back from the field with the rest of the soldiers, somebody reported to the chief that she had been mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How so? How was she mistreated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: She had been raped; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: She was raped repeatedly while she was there, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't learn anything about that case, who raped her, how many times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the last sentence by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last sentence. You said: "I didn't learn anything about that case, who raped her, how many times." What did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not deal with that case because I didn't have access. I couldn't investigate who was in question or what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But this was reported to the Commander Miso Pelemis; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he punished that soldier. I know that he was beaten, that a report was drafted and present -- submitted to the brigade. That's all I know about that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Svetozar Andric would have known about it as well as the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who is --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Svetozar, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who is this person that was punished, the person that did the raping?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a man from the brigade, from the brigade, from the group of people who were on the line. I don't have a list. I don't know. There were people there who had come from the outside, who were displaced. I didn't look into that. Simply, for me, as far as I was concerned ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard from Miso Pelemis. We know that this was a small group of individuals and a small unit. You've described hearing about the raping and you've described hearing about the punishment, the beating of the soldier that did it. We know there is a name in your head. Tell us that name of the soldier that did the beating -- excuse me, that did the raping.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many names of officers and soldiers in my head, the war lasted for four years, and I would not want to do an injustice to any of those people and regret it the next day. I did not conduct an investigation about the case. There are records about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you here. No one asked you whether you investigated. Have you ever heard a name of a person who committed that rape? If so, tell us what name you heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Little Ferida Osmanovic, a 16-year-old, was found in a mass grave within 5 kilometres of Pelemisi with 59 other people. How did she get there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please believe me when I say that I don't know whether she was returned to Vlasenica again or taken from Vlasenica. I cannot comment. I wasn't there. I am a member of the assault detachment that -- in Vlasenica. I went to Pelemisi from time to time to see my family where my wife and my son were. I didn't go to the line until 1993 when the line fell for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the other three women that were found in that mass grave? They were in their 20s. Aida Karac, her sister Velida Karac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Minka, Minka Mehanovic. You remember Minka, don't you? How did she end up in that mass grave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Too many mass graves, too many rapes. Is that why you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that I did not hurt anyone and that I can stand before anyone. All those who were there, who met me, who got to me from the Muslim ethnic group, I am available to all of them. I cannot comment on who did what. I don't have information about that. We all need to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I've one or more questions for you. Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- what Mr. McCloskey now put to you, that women were found in mass graves, even young females. Have you heard about that before, or is it entirely new to you that you hear all this and you say: Well, I wasn't there. I can't explain. But did you hear that before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the excavation of the graves began, of course I heard about it. The whole municipality, the whole country knew about it. This was behind our lines. I didn't go there. The line was in front of the Pelemisi and this happened behind the lines. There is the Vlasenica-Sekovici-Zvornik road. Anybody could kill anybody overnight or transfer them so nobody would know about it. I didn't do any of that. I cannot comment on it. I was there. I can talk about things that I knew -- know about. I cannot talk about things that I don't know about. I'm not a direct participant or perpetrator in the comings and goings there. I sent these people off to Kladanj and, as I say again, they're all still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you're talking about the people you dealt with directly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for those you did not deal with directly, could you tell us that mass grave, and -- was that within the territory controlled by the Serb forces, or was it within the territory at the time controlled by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was territory that was controlled by the Serbian army but behind the line of the Serbian soldiers. I don't know what was happening behind the line, what was done, when was done, in -- when it was done, in which period. I lived my life around Vlasenica and the assault detachment. That's where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you this because in your testimony earlier, you depicted the situation as one of respect and not harming any civilians; whereas, if I understand you well, that you at least learned about that not all civilians were treated in the way as you described the others and that they were found in mass graves. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the civilians that I had anything to do with, the civilians that I met during the war, they're all alive. I can give you their first and last names. Muras Mazelovic [phoen], Nadja from Srebrenica. With this group that I took through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you there. I wasn't asking about the ones you dealt with personally, but you told us also about the fate of others and what happened to them, although not with details, and you didn't tell us at that time that at least you learned that some of those you did not deal with directly, that they ended up in mass graves; whereas, I now understand that you learned that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to know. Once the excavations began, I read about it in the newspaper. A grave found in Pelemis. I saw it on television. But I wasn't there myself. I learned about it all from the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, how did you come to know that the soldier who raped Ferida Osmanovic was beaten?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You heard immediately along the whole line. As soon as they bring the food, you find out what's going on in the village. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you understood my question. I'm talking about the soldier you told us was beaten as punishment for raping Ferida Osmanovic. I'm asking you how did you know that he was beaten for that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole line was talking about it, that he had been beaten because of the rape. The entire Serbian line guarding Pelemisi knew why he was beaten and why he was driven away from the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And he was known, who he was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure -- do you -- do you also know his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many things that were known and many things that were not known. I personally didn't know that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm not asking you about many things that were known. I want to know if you knew this man. He was a soldier with you in the same unit. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a member of my unit. In my unit, none of the soldiers did anything in front of me, nor do I -- nor am I aware that they did anything improper. He was a member of the Trnovska Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. I'm sorry to have said he belonged to your unit. But you were -- he was at the same base as you were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not my soldier. He was somebody else's soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I haven't suggested that now. I said I understand that you say he was not a part of your unit. But he was in the same base where Ferida was detained and where other women were detained and where you also worked, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not saying you were with him. I'm saying he was based at the same area, in the same place where you were based, at the camp where these people were detained. You brought another group there and took it away.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was not a camp. It was a private house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A store.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whatever it was, you were there, he was there. This lady was raped there. I'm not suggesting [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment when the girl was raped, I was not there. I told you quite loud and clear that I was on a mission, and when I returned from the mission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can just listen to my question. I'm not asking whether you saw him rape. I'm asking how you came to know that he was beaten. You say it was all known about the line, and I'm saying who was the person who was said to have been beaten. That's the question I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name. There were a lot of soldiers. I don't want to transgress against anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Mr. Todorovic, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're about to take a break. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness immediately after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume -- Mr. McCloskey, there was one item left yesterday where there were some objections. Is that what you want to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. 65 ter 31647, if -- it was assigned P07381. If that objection is still present, I will withdraw it. Perhaps Mr. Lukic would not object and it will come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we will maintain the same objections, Your Honour, because we have to see what kind of document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we could just MFI that and we'll get back to it at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. I don't know whether the number was reserved or whether it was MFI'd. Mr. Registrar, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number was assigned, Your Honours, but there was an objection in between so -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we have not yet ... 65 ter 31647 received number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7381, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7381. And is marked for identification. When could we hear from the parties so that it doesn't remain forever on our pending issues list. This week, Mr. Lukic? That's on the record. We take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the next witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a digression while we're waiting for the witness. She cannot read very well, so instead of asking her to read the solemn declaration, maybe you should actually say the words first and ask her to repeat after you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is it a matter of sight, or is it a matter of literacy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, and therefore I'll first speak those words and invite you to repeat them, and I'll take it in small portions. Could you please repeat the following words: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I'll speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic standing to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Carefully listen to his questions and please answer them. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slowly tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: My name is Slavka Matic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber where and when were you born.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1944 in Srebrenica municipality, Opati village. Is that what you wanted me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, where did you reside before 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I resided in Bjelovac village, Bjelovac local commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Madam, do you remember the date - that is month and the day - on which you were born in 1944?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 10th -- on the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, who did you live with in 1992 in Bjelovac village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I lived with my family: My husband Radivoje, my older daughter Snezana, my younger daughter Gordana.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember and can you tell the Trial Chamber what was the year of birth of your husband, Radivoje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: He was born in 1937. I believe that he was born in the month of January, but that's all -- I can't remember the date when he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was your daughter Snezana born?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: In 1965, on the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about your younger daughter, Gordana, when was she born?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: In 1967. Also in the month of June but on the 9th. She was born on the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where you were when the war broke out in Srebrenica and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was in my family house. I had always lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you work at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. And then during the war, I was working in the kitchen. I volunteered and I distributed food to the guards and everybody else. To the locals as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about your husband? Was Radivoje employed before the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, he worked at the Sase mine in Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your village, before the month of December 1992, were there any fightings, shootings, and military activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. There were village guards. There was sporadic shooting at us. Our men responded and that went on up to the 14th December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, before December 1992, your husband and your daughters, did they live with you in Bjelovac? Did you all live together?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was your husband militarily engaged in any way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. Because he also kept guard during the night. I never asked him what he did there, but I know that he did keep guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far from your village and from your houses were the positions of the enemy from which shots came?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how far they were in kilometres. As the crow flies, it would have been about a kilometre and a half or 2, tops.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain to the Trial Chamber what you did with regard to the distribution of food during the first months of the war. How was that organised?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: For example, we received dry foods and then we distributed those to the guards, and that went on for perhaps a couple months during the months of May and June. And then later - I don't know when exactly, I don't know the date - we had a kitchen installed in the school because the other villages Loznica, Sikiric, which were a bit further away from us, had been expelled, people were dying there, so those people came down to the field where our village was by the Drina river. Our village is in a valley by a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally prepare food in that school or did you just distribute it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, with a neighbour of mine who was there with me. We would prepare cabbage, potatoes, beans, things like that, and then we would distribute those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your examination will be short. Therefore, I will ask you to tell us where you were in the morning on the 14th December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was at home. I got up at quarter past 6.00 because I worked in the first shift. I had to go there and distribute breakfast together with my neighbour. That was at 6.15. I left the house and then I walked towards the school. I was halfway there. I had a wrist-watch. Shooting started. I didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. Where were you physically when that shooting started?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Some 250 to 300 metres away from my house, on the way to the school. Because my house was 700 metres away from the school. In other words, less than a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did the shots come from? From which direction?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I can't really explain. It came from all over the place. On the left of my house is a hilltop and a forest, and on the right-hand side is the Drina river. So the shooting covered the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do? Where did you find yourself after that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I continued walking towards the school. As I approached the school, bullets started flying and hitting the school. I could hear the tiles on the roof breaking. I hurried up. I entered the school. My neighbour was already there. She arrived before me. I told her to switch off the light because somebody was shooting. I didn't know why. I didn't know who. I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So did she do that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did. As a matter of fact, I switched off the light although I told her to do it. As I entered through the door, I switched off the light.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there while the shooting was going on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I suppose I stayed there some ten minutes. I couldn't leave the school because bullets were fired towards the school, towards the roof of the school. And then I left the school. My cousin lived some 30 or 40 metres away from the school. I went to see him and to tell him that something was going on, that there were shots from all over the place, and he was taken by surprise. He left his house. He got out. And he went -- I don't know where he went. And then I returned to the school somehow. We didn't dare switch on the light. But the light was no longer necessary because it was already daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What's the name of your cousin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Milisav Ilic. He got killed on that day. He went to a place not far from the school to save Cvetjko Lukic who had been seriously injured. He wanted to carry him to the Drina to Ljubovija where he would be safe and he was killed on the boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any locals or the troops or the Serbian police in the village on that morning?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. There were just locals. And by the time those locals got to grips what -- with what was going on, before they could properly wake up, they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you start going back to your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. I set out to my house to see what was going on because I couldn't learn anything from anybody. I saw houses ablaze. I saw smoke. I followed the canal. On the left-hand side of the school, there was a clear -- a clearing, so I could go through there. The asphalt road is somewhat higher, so I crawled and I arrived at a heap of blocks below a house. I stayed there a little. And then on the left-hand side, I saw that Nikola Petrovic's house was ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of the attackers at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw behind that pile of blocks, I peaked over, and then I pulled back. I didn't dare look anymore. I could see three of them standing at the corner of Nikola Petrovic's house. One was on the left side, the other was on the right side. I don't know if they noticed me or not, but because his house was perhaps about 200 metres away from the pile of blocks where I was hiding, I was not able to recognise if it was any of my Muslim neighbours. I couldn't recognise them, but I did see them. I could see well that they had back-packs on their backs. They had some sort of ribbon, yellow perhaps, and the clothing. But that day it was so dark and there was a lot of fog so that had they been only 30 metres in front of me, I would have been able to see if it was -- if it was anybody that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point, did you manage to get through and reach your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. Because on the right-hand side, I could hear a man shouting. I recognised him. For many years we had been at the local commune together when I was there. I was there for 15 years. I had been elected as a functionary of the women's association, the AFZ. I recognised him, Hajrudin Afric. He said, "Chetniks, surrender. We will catch all of you alive." I recognised his voice but he was in the woods, on the right-hand side behind the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were leaving your house and going in the direction of the school in order to distribute the food, who was left in your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: My husband was left behind, Radivoje. My daughter Snezana. My daughters were sleeping when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you manage to get back to your house then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I didn't manage to get back that day, but I was close by because some two or three houses -- three houses in front of me -- my house were burning. I could see that the house of Radovan Vucetic was burning, the house of Dragoljub Filipovic was burning. Dragoljub was killed that day as well. His son Dragan was also killed that day. Radovan Vucetic was killed. His son Milenko, who was 16 or 17, was also killed that day. In any event, he was underaged. Their houses were burning. It was some 30 metres next to my house. I was behind the summer kitchen of Bozo Todorovic. I saw him dead on his terrace. I was at that summer kitchen. That's where I was hiding, but I couldn't reach my own house. And from that place, I saw a man dead on the corner of my own house. I didn't know who it was. I couldn't recognise. Then I saw something else. I had an apple tree in front of my house. There was a man lying there. I recognised that it was my husband. I could tell by his clothes. He had a kind of yellowish jacket. Actually, it was the olive-drab, the SNB colour. I could recognise him. I saw that he was killed. I didn't know anything about the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when was the first time that you managed to enter your yard and get to your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: It was only the next day because they wouldn't let me. They turned me back. A man called me, "Don't go there. That's where the Muslims were stationed, those attackers. You mustn't go there." And since I was by myself, I went back some 20 metres, and then I reached that man, and that was Srecko Mihajlovic. He was sitting in the canal underneath the plum tree. I asked him about my family, my relatives, did he know what happened to them, and he told me that all three of them were killed, although I recognised my husband but I couldn't see my children. Then there was some two or three men there, I can't remember who they were. I don't remember who they were to this day. They turned me back. They told me, "You mustn't go there. It's not safe." They told me to go to a house where I spent the whole night, and then the next day help arrived. I don't know who it was, what that was. They took me to my house at about 9.30. That was the following day. The 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just bear with us. We don't want to upset you more than we have to. But could you tell us, as briefly as possible, what you saw when you went back to your house.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I found my daughter, Snezana, lying next to the staircase on the floor. Then when I entered the house, I found a large pool of blood. I didn't know where my youngest daughter was, my daughter Gordana. I walked around the house, and you can imagine how it was for me, what happened to me, and how I behaved. I found her dead in the bathroom. She had bled to death because she didn't get any help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were any buildings in your yard damaged or burned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: My house was set on fire that day, but there was a woman there who came to help my children. She wasn't able to. It wasn't possible because the house was surrounded, but she managed to put out the fire so that the children, my children wouldn't burn. And then when we collected the dead on the following day so that we could bury them on the 16th in Bratunac, they returned again and torched everything. So on the 16th, everything was torched. All that that was there of mine. It was all torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you buried your son [as interpreted] and your two daughters then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: At the Bratunac town cemetery. We had to transport them all in the boat, and then we went to Bratunac to the cemetery because there were blocks, there were ambushes on all sides, and we couldn't go up or down the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to finish with this question. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber how many inhabitants of your village were killed that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: 68 were killed that day. Among those 68 people, there were nine women -- actually, ten. The tenth one is -- her whereabouts are still unknown. That was Bozana Ostojic. She was perhaps 70 years old. She didn't have children. One of her brothers was killed. One of her brothers died. One of her cousins was killed. Another one died. All in the war. So there's nobody to actually look for her. She was never found and we don't know what happened to her. She was my sister-in-law, my husband's first cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us where you lived in the months and years after that, in view of the state of your house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. One second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a refugee and I lived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you introduced your last question by saying I'm going to finish with this question. That was at the moment when Ms. MacGregor was on her feet. I didn't know what she wanted to tell us, but when she heard that it would be your last question I think she sat down again. Could I inquire with you now, how many more questions do you have? Because we hear a lot of details, and I'm fully aware that -- how it affected your personal life, but of course we also have to keep in mind the relevance for this case, and sometimes events which have a huge impact on personal lives are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have four more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. When Mr. Stojanovic put a question to the witness, he asked about her -- it was either a mistranslation or mistake on his part. He asked about her son. I think he probably meant to refer to her husband, so I just wanted to correct the record. That was at -- on page 37.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Line 8, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, the question was translated -- it was interpreted by us as: "Could you please tell us where you buried your son and your two daughters." Is that what you intended to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. If I said "son," then I made an error. But I think that I said something different. I can clear that up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do it immediately. When you told us that members of your family were buried at the Bratunac town cemetery, did you refer to your two daughters and your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you before this intervention was where did you live in the months and years that ensued in view of the state of your houses and your household?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I lived in Bratunac in an apartment - I don't know whose apartment it was - until 1997, and since I wasn't able to return earlier because everything had been burned, I waited until everything was rebuilt so that I could go and live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how are you living now and who are you living with?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I live alone. I live alone. As they say, like a tree with no branches. That's what my life is like today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me your closest relatives who were -- and the people who were killed that day, how did they comment that attack by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: From what I could hear from my relatives, my neighbours whose son, brother, father, sister, were killed, that out of outrage, they were outraged, I don't know why this place was attacked when our neighbours, our people, my family, nobody ever ventured into those other villages. In 1992, as far as I can remember, and judging by the stories that we heard, 40 villages were emptied in the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities. They killed what they could. People who managed to escape, escaped. They spent some time with us for a while, men, women, until they could manage to find another place, go and stay with their families. I had family in Spati [phoen] in Zaluzje. I had family in Brezani. I had a very large family on my mother's side, but all of those villages were wiped out in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to finish with this question. How do you view your neighbours, your Muslim neighbours, today, the people who are living in your immediate neighbourhood? What is your personal attitude towards all these things?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: What is my attitude? What they did to me, I would have never done that to them, and I never could imagine that they could do something like that to me. They knew me well. They knew that there were no soldiers at my place, that I had daughters. I don't know why this happened, what the reason was. I can never forget it. I don't know if I can or cannot forgive them. I'm still thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Slavka, thank you very much for your efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honours, for the time we have been allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. One final matter, Mr. Stojanovic, Slavka, is that short for the official first name or is it the official first name of the witness, to the extent you are aware of? Is that Slavka your official name or is that a short version of your ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my full name. Slavka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. MacGregor, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Matic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. MacGregor. You'll find Ms. MacGregor to your right, and Ms. MacGregor is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Matic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have a couple of general questions about the Bratunac municipality. If you know, before the war started, the majority of the people in Bratunac municipality were Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't answer that. I never dealt much in politics. I didn't know what the figures were. I really couldn't say. Perhaps it's true. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- unless it is a useful introduction to your follow-up questions, typically a matter to be agreed upon by the parties. We have the 1991 census which would most likely will give an answer to that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have one question further on that that's not addressed by the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And it's more particular, Madam Matic, to the hamlets directly around Bjelovac. Is it correct that the hamlets of Pirici and Skela [phoen] were predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pirici, Goradze, and Poloznik. Those were purely Muslim villages. It's a bit further away from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And moving on to the events in December 1992 that you've been discussing, you've described a guard in your village today during your testimony. Did the members of those guards wear civilian clothes or uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, sometime in the month of June, some had uniforms, but most wore civilian clothes. Some men did have camouflage uniforms. We didn't. We were villagers. We had village guards. We didn't have troops. There were few men who had camouflage uniforms. Perhaps the younger ones. The older ones, like my husband and others, wore their civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And is it correct that if those individuals had their own weapons, say, a hunting rifle or something like that, that they would use those weapons when they were guarding the village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, did your daughters participate in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And do you know, on the day of the attack, on 14 December, 1992, did the village guard fight back against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The village came under attack. If there had been no resistance, perhaps they would have killed everybody. They killed a lot of people. Minors, women, they killed, for example --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: -- nine women in my village on that day. And then on the 28th of June in Loznica, Jela Stojanovic was killed and Verica Filipovic. She was also a minor. And perhaps nine more were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Madam, if I can ask you to just listen to the questions I'm asking and try to focus your answers to those questions, and then hopefully we can be done quite soon.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, is it correct on the day, on 14 December, 1992, at some point during that day you sought shelter in an APC; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When I say "APC," I'm referring to a vehicle. Did you get into a vehicle on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember. There weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Today you testified that 68 individuals were killed during the fighting in Bjelovac in December 1994. Now, do you know of those 68 people how many of the Serb victims of -- how many of these people were soldiers and how many were civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 43, line 24, I'm not sure about the date as recorded. What the witness heard in the interpretation was what is recorded on the transcript, which I'm afraid can cause some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, apparently there may be a problem, but could you also keep in mind the reference to the 68 is found in page 37, line 17, and does not read exactly as you put it to the witness. Could you please keep that in mind as well if you, again, put a question about the 68 to the witness. Especially what occurs after: "During..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Madam, according to your testimony, 68 people were killed in Bjelovac on 14th of December, 1994 -- excuse me, 1992. Now, do you know of those 68 people how many were soldiers and how many were civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: There were more civilians than soldiers and those who had been mobilised were the local youth; for example, Mirko Petrovic, and then Damjanovic - what's his face? - I forgot his name. They were killed. Dragan Filipovic. Younger people. I suppose that they were soldiers. Probably they had been mobilised. And there were others whose names I can't remember, but most were civilians. The elderly, women, and even the men; for example, Ljubisav Nedeljkovic, he was over 60 years old. Desimir Matovic was also around 60. They were all around 50 or 60 years of age. And then there was this guy Prodanovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please see 65 ter 4415.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And, madam, on your screen I know that you won't necessarily be able to see it, but what I'm showing to the Chamber is a report that's written by the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I can't see a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I understand, and I'm going to read to you from this document. What I -- I want to describe what it is to you. It's a report that the military make. It's a report specifically from the Bratunac Brigade, and it gives a history of how the brigade was formed and what fighting it was involved in. So I want to read to you from this report briefly because the report speaks specifically about the fighting on the 14th of December, 1992, in your village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, the document apparently starts with D-10. That doesn't -- is not in the same script. Could you explain to us what exactly we're looking at apart from, of course, telling the witness, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see a thing. What do you want me to do? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything will be explained to you, Witness. If you wait for a second, I had a small question for the -- for Ms. MacGregor, and we'll deal with that first, and then just bear with us for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm understanding your question. If you want to hear more about what larger document this is part of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether -- first of all, I do not know whether it's part of a larger document. What I do know is that I see a document in Cyrillic script with a -- in a totally different typewriting D-10 on top of it. I don't see any specific cover page with dates, et cetera, so I'm wondering what I'm looking at at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that this is how the document appeared, it seems, when the -- when OTP seized it. It's a document that has actually been referred to in testimony here before Your Honours, although not admitted into evidence. I can get back to you with a bit more detail at a later time if you want. I won't be tendering this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
