utterances.text: Then please proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Madam Matic, I'm going to go -- if we can please go to page 11 in the English and on the Cyrillic, it's in page 10. And it's about halfway down that I'll start reading. In the paragraph that begins: "On 14 December 1992, the Muslims attacked the villages of Sikiric, Loznica, Biljaca, Bjelovac, and Voljavica on the left flank. The villages suffered huge material," and I presume there's a word missing there, "the villages suffered huge material and many people were killed. 55 soldiers and 7 civilians were killed and many were wounded in the fighting with the units of Naser Oric. All villages were torched and the property destroyed." Madam, have you heard what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, this document has 55 soldiers and seven civilians killed during the fighting, which is 63 people. Now, according to the document made by the military, 55 of those Serbs --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: 55 of those Serbs that died in the fighting were soldiers. Now, do you think that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: There were soldiers. I know that there were. But there were more civilian casualties. I don't know what they wrote about the incident, how they reported about it, but as far as I know, and as much as I know about my village, I -- I know who -- who was killed on that day. And there were a lot of elderly and women among them. There were even woman who were injured who succumbed one or two years later and died of the -- of those wounds. I don't know. And now as to how reports were drafted, what was written after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can next have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "the military." Could you at least tell us what military we are talking about? Is it the British Army or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The locals who were there who had been mobilised. If they were of age. We did not have any other troops. We didn't have any such thing. Those people were just there and if -- if anybody thought of them as troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that last question I put to Ms. MacGregor, and I'm still waiting for at least some information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, my question was about members of the -- of the Serb military. My question to the witness. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question to you was when you said this is a military report, from what military? As far as you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's from the Bratunac Brigade of the VRS. This document was used by Ms. Melikian and she also gave to Your Honours some information about the background of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I must say I don't have a clear recollection of that, I must admit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It was on 30 April of this year, 2015, with Witness Ratko Nikolic. It was seized in a search executed by the ICTY in February 1995 from the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's one document, 22 pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The full document -- I'm sorry, can you please repeat your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's one document or whether it's several documents and is all the 22 pages are one document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I would have to spend more time looking into this. But as I understand, what we've uploaded is a portion of the document and not the entire collection that was seized. But again, I can get back to you about that. But not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you would then also explain to us where we find that it's a document which is coming from the Bratunac Brigade, that would be appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I can please have 65 ter -- excuse me for one moment. 04254.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Madam, I'm asking the court usher to show to the Chamber another document, and I know you will probably also have trouble seeing it, so it's actually a document that you were shown when you testified here in the Naser Oric trial. And we're just waiting for it to come up to the screen. But as we wait, I'll tell you that this is a list that's entitled: "List of Soldiers of 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade Killed Between 18 April 1992 and 25 September 1995."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, before you put questions to the witness, could you tell us how much more time you would need, because we're -- I'm looking at the clock at this moment and it's approximately time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This is my final document about which -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the final document, then I'll suggest that we'll wait until we have concluded this portion and then take the break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, if we can please turn to page 3 in the B/C/S and 4 in the English, we're going to look at number 260 on this list. And, Madam, I believe you had trouble seeing it, but I also think you were shown this before in the Oric case --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I can't read.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to read. Ms. MacGregor will explain exactly what it is that is before you, and anything you're invited to comment upon, she'll read that literally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I will read entry number 260. The name that's listed is Matic, son of Ilija, Radivoje. The unit listed is --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- 3rd Infantry Battalion. The date of birth, 1937. The address listed is Bjelovac. Place of death is Bjelovac. The date of death, 14 December 1992. And under remarks, it says: "In action (defence)." Is that your husband whose information I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please turn to 6 in e-court in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you, Madam, entries 415 and 416.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This may be the wrong English page unless -- it should be page 7 then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. Starting with line 415, the name is Matic, Radivoje, Gordana. The unit is the letters OT. The date of birth is 1967. The address is Bjelovac. The place of death is Bjelovac. The date of death is 14 December 1992. And under remarks it lists: "In action (defence)." And is that your daughter Gordana?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And entry number 416 is the same as the entry for Gordana, with just three differences: The name is Matic, daughter of Radivoje, well, actually, it says Radivoje, Snezana, and the date of birth listed for her is 1965. Now, is that your daughter Snezana?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, this document lists that your husband and your daughters were killed in action, and it lists them on a list of members of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Were you aware that your husband and daughters were members of that brigade when they died?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My husband, I never asked him, and I suppose so. I never knew that my daughter had been mobilised or what. I really didn't know until I came here in 2004 and when that was shown to me. I was against that. I wanted to move them away. Who mobilised them and how they accepted that? They did not die in combat. They died at home. They didn't have even a stick in their hands let alone something else that they could defend themselves with. What could they have defended themselves with? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7383, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Prosecution has no further questions. I can provide a bit more information about the Bratunac Brigade documents now or I can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, let's firstly -- my first question to you, Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions in re-examination for the witness? And, if so, we'll wait until after the break. But if you don't have any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't have any. But I would like to clarify with the OTP the abbreviation OT. What is the position of the Prosecutor on that, based on the document they have just tendered into evidence? I would like to learn from them about their understanding of the nature of that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we cannot agree on that, I will have a couple of questions for the witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I'm wondering where the witness says that she was not aware of her family members being members of the armed forces whether the witness could help us out. But let's first hear from Ms. MacGregor whether she -- how she understands the abbreviation OT in the document, which was just admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've had some discussions with members of the CLSS and I have a couple ideas, but I'm not in a position to say the final position of the Prosecution. I'm happy to talk to the Defence at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then, of course, if the witness has been excused, then we can't ask her. Now, Mr. Stojanovic, is there any reason why you think that this witness could help us out in view of the previous answers she gave about her family members?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I spoke with the witness about that, and I don't think that she can be of any assistance to us. She told us what she knew and she gave us the full extent of her knowledge, so I don't think it would be necessary to keep her to stay after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means, if you say I have a few more questions, it's rather questions for Ms. MacGregor than for the witness. In view of that, no further questions in re-examination, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that the OT matter remains unresolved at this moment. Madam Matic, this concludes your evidence in this Court, and I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague. It may not have been easy for you to be taken back to days that were certainly difficult, very difficult, in your life. I wish you a safe return home again and thank you again for having answered all the questions that were put to you. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at half past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the -- yes, perhaps we wait for one second, Mr. Usher. Ms. MacGregor, you wanted to give us a bit of background information about that one document which you did not tender.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I also have information about the OT debate. So I'll start with the simpler matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This is the document number P7383 and the document that's 65 ter 04415. So 04415 is the Bratunac Brigade history document that we discussed. P7383 is the list of deaths that was entered into evidence. Both of these documents were seized by the OTP in a search in February 1998, and they were seized from the Bratunac Brigade. So that's the information about those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then OT stands in your view for?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This is a bit more complicated. So to assist the Chamber, if I can ask to put on the screen, 65 ter 32581. And, Your Honours, this is a document that the Prosecution decided not to use with the witness but it was on the exhibit list, and it's -- I'm waiting for it to come up. It's a document dated October 1992, list of persons from military post 2465/5, paid for official troop trip and pay for October 1992. It's a list of persons to whom payments were made. If you go to page 7, and we can actually just look at the B/C/S because it's a list and because we're talking about the initials and they refer to B/C/S language. At the top of this list, we see the words "Oklopno Mehaniz Jedinica", which our translation is "armoured mechanized unit," obviously with the second word abbreviated. And if you look on this list at numbers 233 and 234, you see the names of Madam Matic's daughters, who we discussed during her testimony. Additionally, there are five other individuals on this list that we're looking at who are also listed on the list of dead individuals in Exhibit P7383 who also have the initial OT next to their name. So the conclusion of the Prosecution is that O stands for "Oklopno." I don't know what word T stands for, but our understanding is that this is a reference to the armoured mechanized unit that the two sisters and these other five individuals belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic -- first of all, this, of course, is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further comments on the OT issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have also analysed this abbreviation while I was preparing for the witness's testimony, also bearing in mind the line of questions that the witness had during the cross-examination in the Oric case. I couldn't hear from her anything that could help me to identify and explain the abbreviation OT. That's why I said that she couldn't be of any assistance to us. It is our position that the abbreviation for the anti-armour mechanical unit in military terms cannot be OT. However, as for the real meaning of the abbreviation OT, we are not in a position to answer to that question right now. We shall try and see if we can clarify this with some of the upcoming issues, and then we will take it up with OTP and see whether they can stipulate anything with regard to that abbreviation and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Do the parties agree that OT refers to a unit within that brigade or is there even no agreement on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will continue to look to try to sort this out. But it -- it -- the Prosecution is really not attempting to prove whether or not these women are in the -- in the unit or not, but we did want you to see that evidence so that this could be seen in context. It's not an issue that the Prosecution, as you know, feels it needs to prove, but we did want to give you the context. And as we can answer your questions, we will, and we'll continue to look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll hear further from the parties in the future. Could the next witness be escorted in the courtroom, unless, Ms. MacGregor, you would like to raise any matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I was just going to ask if I may have your permission to depart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher will open the door anyhow, so you can use that opportunity to leave this courtroom. You're excused, Ms. MacGregor. Next witness to be called would be Mr. Radulj?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radulj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Radulj. You'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, and you'll find him to your left, is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radulj.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to our procedure, I would kindly ask you to slowly tell us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Slobodan Radulj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, could you give us the date and place of your birth.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: 17 July, 1956. I was born in Verici, in Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you currently reside, Mr. Radulj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I reside in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation at the moment and what is your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I am the ombudsman of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber something about your education.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I completed the elementary school in the place where I was born. I attended the secondary school in Banja Luka. I graduated from the school of law in Banja Luka in 1978. After that, I went to Novi Sad, and I took my bar exam there in 1991. In 2004, I completed the specialist post-graduate studies about organised crime and fight against terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: And then in 2007, I obtained my masters degree in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask you to tell us something about your professional career from the moment when you obtained your first law degree until today.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I got my first job in 1978 at the Ljubija-Prijedor iron-ore mine because I had a study grant from that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how long did you stay with that company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I worked as a lawyer from 1978 to September 1991 in that company. I was the company lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, in September 1991, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: In September 1991, I got call-up papers and I was mobilised into the rocket unit of the then-JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was that unit stationed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: That unit arrived from Banja Luka in the territory of today's Croatia. It was stationed in the territory covered by Dvor na Uni, Glina, and Petrinja. To be more precise, the name of that area is Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, in September 1991, did you have any military education? Did you have a military rank?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's stop there. Let's stop talking about your professional career. Tell us about your military education and also tell us where did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I served in Bileca at the school of reserve officers there. I became a second lieutenant after the completion of that education. At the moment when I was mobilised, I was a reserve captain, a reserve infantry captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did your military engagement last, in that unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I was in Croatia until the 11th of April, 1992; and after that, until the 15th of May, 1992, I was in Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber which unit you belonged to until the 15th of May, 1992 in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: It was the same rocket brigade, which had returned from Croatia to the Celinac-Prnjavor sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat -- ah okay. You don't need to. I think it's been recorded. What I want to ask you is this: How long were you engaged in this unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I already said that. I was there until the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, what new duties did you take up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: While I was at the unit, I was summoned to Prijedor to take over the duties of the municipal ombudsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you take up those duties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I took up those duties on the 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at that post?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I stayed at that post until the 20th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where you went after the 20th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: From the 20th of October, 1993, I was appointed Deputy Military Prosecutor for the area of responsibility of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at that post?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I stayed at the post of deputy until the 1st of August, 1997, and then after that, I was appointed as prosecutor of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at that post?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I was there until the 1st of July, 2000, which was the day when the military judicial system was abolished in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you went from there? What was your job from then until today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: After the year 2000, I started working as an advisor at the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was until 2006. And then after that, in 2007 until now, I am the attorney general of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to draw your attention to a particular time-period that you talked about as the time when you worked as an attorney at the iron-ore mine in Ljubija. For those of us who are not from that area, could you please tell us where the town of Ljubija is located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: The iron-ore company at that time was made up of three mines. One of them was Ljubija. That would be the central mining area. And then that is 12 kilometres south of Prijedor. The second mine is called Istocna Rudista in Tomasica, and that is south-east of Prijedor, some 20 kilometres away. And the third mining sector is Omarska and that is 20 kilometres to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what the ethnic composition of the staff of the company where you worked was up until the beginning of the war, the company where you worked as an attorney?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: The company numbered about 5.000 employees, and they were from among all ethnic groups and ethnic minorities. In electing the management organs, the key system was always taken into account, meaning that certain posts -- meaning that all ethnic groups were equally represented in all the posts. The management posts. The situation was more than good. The company was operating very well, and the salaries were good. It was a pleasure to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the situation was good, I wanted to ask you more specifically about the interethnic relations in your company.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Before the multi-party elections, they were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after the multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, the SDA won in the Prijedor municipality, that was the Muslim option, and that's when changes occurred. There was a deterioration in the political and the interethnic situation. There was more and more distrust among the inhabitants as well. Specifically, the Serb citizens were more disturbed. I specifically had a lot of unpleasantness because of that because, in my view, the main differences were those who were in favour of the survival of Yugoslavia and those who were in favour of dismantling it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put some questions to you later on about that, so we need to go step by step. That's what the system is here. When you say that people had a different attitude towards the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what you personally observed? You personally.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I am just going to give two or three examples. One of them is the case of my colleague, an economist by profession, Zoran Pusac, who brought a report to the collegium. The director was Ibro Paunovic. The report was written in the Cyrillic script. And when the director saw the Cyrillic script, he ripped up the report as a gesture and he said: "I do not want to see Cyrillic in this company anymore." The second case was when I received a warning from colleagues about when I brought in the morning press in the morning that I was -- that I should hide it. I asked why, and they told me that the porters had been given an assignment to note down who was bringing in what kind of newspapers in the morning. Cyrillic or the Belgrade newspapers were undesirable, and I actually happened to read the Belgrade press. I still have a lot of Muslim friends to this day, and once when we were just having drinks, one of them who is a good friend of mine said this: "Yugoslavia is no more. Serbs should go to Serbia, Croats should go to Croatia, Bosnia is ours." If I may add something else too. When I talked about nice times in Prijedor or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the formula that was in force then was that Bosnia and Herzegovina was Muslim, Serb, and Croat; namely, Bosnia and Herzegovina was neither Serb nor Muslim nor Croat. That formula could apply for as long as Yugoslavia existed. The minute that Yugoslavia disappeared, that formula was no longer valid, and that is when these conflicts broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you to give us a time context for these three or four specific examples that you mentioned. When did they take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: This already started in the late 1990s, in the course of 1991 and in early 1992. As time went by, this intolerance among the peoples became more and more pronounced. I can even say that the Serbian people were upset because of the historic -- because of past history.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what do you mean when you say "past history"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: The historic memory whereby Kozara is close. Mount Kozara is in the Prijedor area, and there is Jasenovac camp also in that area, meaning that only 40 years before that horrific crimes were committed against the Serbian people. So that in May and June of 1942, 70.000 men, women, and children died in that area. Out of that, 40.000 were children under -- under 14. When I was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 20.000, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was small, in one day, 520 civilians were killed alone. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little bit here. That's being suggested. I'm sorry, you can continue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stojanovic, you are aware that this is evidence which is repeated so many times. You're encouraged to avoid repetitious evidence, and it also seems that -- that a lot of Serbs were suffering heavily during the Second World War is not something which is in dispute, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for the suggestion, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is the first time that this concrete information has been stated. I am just going to ask to you finish your sentence and then I will move to the next question. So we interrupted you at the point in time when you were talking about numbers that refer to your own village.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: What I said was that because of fear that history will repeat itself and those crimes, that's what -- what the reason was for their concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And you personally, did you have any experiences in your company immediately before the war broke out that indicated a different approach and attitude towards the then-Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Well, the approach was different. Since I need to stick to the facts, I recall that one tank brigade from Serbia came to Prijedor and that the mayor of Prijedor stood in front of the tanks at the time. I can't remember his name. He was a Muslim. And then on the other hand, the people allowed the Serbian army to come to Prijedor and they were giving them food and water, which means that the -- that already at that time the JNA was not permitted to pass through Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to direct your attention to the period when you started your duties as attorney general of the Prijedor municipality, and I would like to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber briefly what your duties were, what that involved, the job of attorney general at the municipal authority level.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: The position of attorney general is something that I think exists in all countries. In the briefest possible way, you could say that that is an attorney of the state institutions. These were institutions that are financed from the budget, municipal organs, and our job was to make sure that laws and regulations were respected. Its role was to draw attention and make sure that the authorities did not violate laws, and they also took care of citizens' rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you carrying out those duties as a management-level official? Did you have any assistants to help you in your job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I worked alone. I was the only one at that post, and I just had a technical secretary. Even before me, my colleague, my predecessor worked by himself. He was the only -- or me, too, the only professional official in that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were doing your job, was it your duty to attend meetings of the local assembly or of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: No, I was not obliged to attend those meetings, but I was obliged at the request of the president to come to the meetings where items were being dealt with that had to do with my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you aware of the work of the Crisis Staff in the Prijedor municipality at any point in time while you were attorney general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I know that there was a Crisis Staff. It was formed while I was still in the unit, and I was not a member of the Crisis Staff so that I didn't have any influence on its work, and I did not participate in any of the duties of the Crisis Staff because the judiciary was separate from the rest of the organs of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what were the most frequent problems that you encountered as the public attorney, the attorney general, up until the time you became Deputy Military Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: What the biggest problem was, was to set up organs of power of any sort. What happened was that state authorities disappeared. The state of Yugoslavia disappeared, as well as the organs of power of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. New organs of power had to be created. They were just emerging so that there was a vacuum which seemed to have been filled with unsavory figures, criminals, crooks thinking that in that lawless period you could do anything you wanted. So in this vacuum all the crimes occurred and all the things that an ordinary man would find difficult to accept, all these things that people were willing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you worked in Prijedor municipality as its attorney general, did you have to bear any pressure with regard to your duty and decisions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: No, there were no pressures to bear. I was an independent body, as it were, so I was the one who issued enactments and documents to demand solutions to current issue, especially property issues. I would say in those documents that that was private property, and in a capitalist society it was inviolable. So even if somebody had to abandon Prijedor due to war, nobody had the right to violate their property. Everybody left Prijedor during the war - Bosniaks, Serb, Croats and Yugoslavs - but their property remained unprotected and that was the main issue, the issue that was close to my heart. I wanted that property to be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the term "abandoned property." Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what was implied under the term "abandoned property" in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Those were socially owned apartments primarily, and houses. There were already some small private companies and stores in Prijedor. All those assets that belonged to the citizens who had been forced to leave the town due to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You observed that as an objective problem. Did you inform companies, institutions, state organs about the problems that you observed when it came to abandoned property?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I drafted several documents that I sent primarily to all the institutions in the municipality. I even asked that a list be published in the local newspaper. I attended sessions, and at those sessions I demanded that laws be observed and that property of others be protected and respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to call up 65 ter 1D05383.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we'll go back to page 1. But before that, I would like us to look at the last page in B/C/S and English versions of this document. Just for a moment, let's focus on that. Let me ask you: At the end of the document, you can see the abbreviation VD, municipal public legal officer, Slobodan Radulj, and a signature. Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I was acting municipal legal officer and this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's go back to the first page of this document. I'll have a few questions for you. This document bearing your signature was drafted on the 21st of September, 1992. Below the date, you can see the words "enterprise or institution." What do these words stand for? What do these words imply in this type of document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: This is a circular letter. My clerk who worked with me would fill in the document by adding the name of the institution or company to which the document was sent. So instead of typing the entire document on an old typewriter, we made a few copies and left blanks for the names of the institutions. This document was published in Kozarski Vjesnik Newspaper so everybody could read this document, both citizens and the institutions to which the document referred, and the document referred to all those who were in any position of authority in the territory of Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is this: Can you personally tell us today whether this document of yours, whether this letter of yours was ever sent to the companies and institutions in the territory of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course, and it was also published. Everybody received this document. I don't know how many addresses were involved. There must have been hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to you look at the second paragraph of this document where you say: "In these conditions some individuals have found ways to take possession of certain property, especially socially-owned flats ... every day we see forcible break-ins and illegal occupation of socially-owned flats ... this has become a large-scale phenomenon." Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what do you mean when you say "socially-owned flats"? What kind of property does this concern or what kind of ownership?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Socially-owned flats at that time were not private property. They did not belong to the tenant who occupied such an apartment. Companies, institutions assigned apartments to their own employees and workers for temporary or permanent occupation. According to the then-prevalent laws, that right of occupation could be lost on a condition that they occupied such an apartment for six months without any justification, without the right of occupancy. In this document, I am warning everybody that this term of six months cannot be applied during the war because their citizens left not of their own will. They would return and they would ask to be allowed to move back into their apartments. Let me tell you that at that moment I couldn't even dream that there would be a Dayton Accord, but this letter is very much in the vain of that accord because after the Dayton Accords were signed, everybody was allowed to return to their former property.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document discriminate along any lines against any of the tenants in the socially-owned apartments, especially along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I believe that the text itself shows, that it is self-explanatory, and it is clear that it applies to all citizens irrespective of their ethnic affiliations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The essence of my question was this: What was the attitude of the official authorities - and you were a member of those authorities at the time, obviously - about who could use and manage an apartment whose tenant had to leave the apartment due to war? Whose apartment was that? Who had the right to occupy it and use it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the term official authorities could be understood to apply to a variety of different institutions, some of which the witness was a member of, some of which he testified he didn't know very much about, so I'd just ask that that term be made a little bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're invited to follow that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I'll see what I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, and I apologise, Mr. Radulj, what was the position of your office within the context of the question that I put to you? Who had the right to use those apartments that you described as abandoned socially-owned apartments? Who was supposed to dispose with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Well, in order for me to answer that, I have to expand a little. I already told that you companies were the owners of such apartments. The municipality also had its own apartments. So the owners had to make sure that the rights of previous tenants had to be respected, that such apartments could not be allocated permanently. Some individuals forcibly entered such apartments. Sometimes individuals even chased away their rightful occupants. So the owners had the obligation to make sure that the previous tenants had their rights reinstated and that is the essence of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us look at page 3, paragraph 1 in the same document. I believe that the same paragraph is found on the same page in the English version as well. Just a moment, Mr. Radulj, we're waiting for the English version to appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the previous page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your letter, you go on to say: "Until then everybody a who has anything to do with this problem should bear in mind the following: "1. All persons who have moved into flats without the requisite decisions issued by the organs responsible for letting flats are," and then highlighted or underscored or, rather, "... illegal occupants who must be evicted in accordance with the Municipal Assembly's decision of 27 August 1992." My question is this: What you have written in this letter, is this your position and your attitude as the attorney general; or rather when you make a reference to the decision of the Municipal Assembly, are you also relying on the position or the attitude of the highest authorities in the municipality? Whose position is this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I really can't remember the details. This was a long time ago, but I believe that this was a decision made by the Municipal Assembly that all the illegal tenants should be evicted. In practice, however, this never took off the ground. However, I issued this document in order to encourage everybody involved to make sure that the decision was indeed carried out. This is the essence of this letter. The decision was not implemented to the extent necessary or possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at bullet point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S we should move to the following page and in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we move to the next point, it's about time for a break, otherwise the last session will be very, very short. Before moving, therefore, I would like to take the break now. Mr. Radulj, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after that break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, we left it off with bullet point 4 in this document. Let's go to the following page in B/C/S. We are on the good page in English because we can see the first two lines of that bullet point but then we have to move on. In this document in this bullet point you say: "Since the war is not yet over and people are still being wounded and killed, it should be realised that there will unfortunately be many more families of fallen warriors and disabled war veterans with no one to support them, and priority will have to be given to the solution of their problem. The above-mentioned decision of the Municipal Assembly places this obligation squarely on the enterprises and institutions responsible for the allocation of socially-owned flats." What was your objective when you sent this document to all the enterprises and institutions of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Primarily my objective was to make sure that law is observed, that there was order, and that individuals who were not entitled to certain benefits should not be allowed to take laws in their own hands. That that job should be given to legal institutions and authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Let me share an example with you to illustrate the whole situation. As an attorney general, I got hold of a sales purchase agreement of a small-sized company. The seller, who was a Croatian lady, Marija Popovic, and the name of her company was Hidroflex, had left Prijedor as far as I knew. The buyer, on the other hand, brought me that purchase agreement that I was supposed to certify in order for the contract to be registered. I refused to certify the contract because I had my doubts about the whole deal. And then I checked the signature of the seller. I matched it against the signature that was on the company inception papers, and I checked the contract itself and I realised that it was a forgery. The property that was left behind was placed at the disposal of the municipality temporarily until the moment the issue could be permanently resolved. Not only did I not put my signature on the contract, but I also filed a claim with a court to make the contract null and void. As a result, I suffered threats from individuals who wanted to abuse state institutions and get hold of valuable property in an illegal way. This is just to illustrate how I wanted to protect it, the assets of everybody irrespective of their ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That person who presented to you as the buyer of the property which was ownership of a Croatian from Prijedor, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: He was a Serb. Actually, they were two brothers who were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During that year while you worked in the attorney general's office, did you have any experiences with ethnic discrimination on behalf of the authorities and the courts in Prijedor when it came to law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: My offices were in the building of the court and the prosecutor's office. I was a professional, and I was only governed by the law. Throughout the -- the duration of my office, I did not allow any discrimination. Very often Bosniaks turned to me for advice or instructions that could help them, and I always obliged as much as I could and as much as I was allowed to do so within the purview of my duties. I believe that the court in Prijedor also did not discriminate against anybody. At least I have not experienced any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's go back to bullet point 4 that can you see in front of you and which is an integral part of your letter. At that time, did you personally know if MUP units or the Army of Republika Srpska units also had members of non-Serb origin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Yes. For example, my unit, which was a motorised company, when I joined, it was a JNA unit. In that unit, there was some ten Muslims, about eight Croats, and other ethnic groups, including Albanians and Yugoslavs. I also know that in the two Prijedor brigades, there were other ethnic groups. There was even a company of Croats in a village near Ljubija. I can't remember the name of that village. I heard stories about that. I can't remember if the name of that village was Ravsko or something else. In any case, it was a Croatian village. Don't hold me by that because I'm not sure. I remember that information about a purely Croatian company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Within the context of your information, i.e., the circular letter that you sent to various institutions, the families of such persons of non-Serb origin, if they were members of the MUP or the Army of Republika Srpska, and if they were injured or if they were killed, would their families also fall within the category of the families of those who had to be taken care of because their members had either been injured or died in combat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Of course. There would have been no discrimination whatsoever. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I ask a few clarifying questions. You talked about your motorised company. You said there were some ten Muslims and about eight Croats. What was the total strength of that company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were around 150 men in my company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said when you joined that unit. Did the composition change after you had joined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I joined the unit in late September 1991. Already at the beginning of 1992, the composition changed. A large number of Muslims and Croats left the unit. At that time, that was considered normal that everybody tended to move closer to their own people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Normal or not, that's not my -- I just wanted to look at the facts. So do I understand the ten -- let me just check that. The ten Muslims and the eight Croats, that was in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many were left in, well, let's say, June 1992; that is, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left the unit on the 15th of May, 1992, but this number then, in my opinion, was halved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that your opinion or were you able to know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure. This is my estimate, free estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be -- well, let me first put another question to you. You talked to us about Muslims and Croats. How many other non-Serbs were there? You said there were -- from other ethnicities as well. How many of those were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that there was one Albanian, then there were active members of the unit, Montenegrins and Slovenians and Macedonians. They were on activity duty, officers and NCOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how many of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember exactly how many because the brigade was much larger. My records were only covering the motorised company, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking you about the company, which you said had a strength of 150. Do I understand that the ten Muslims and the eight Croats, they were in your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how many Montenegrins and Albanians were there in your company or, well, let's say, other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there were two Montenegrins, an Albanian was added. He was an active-duty officer. He was just seconded to the unit, but it was just for a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, approximately it was 85 per cent Serbs and 15 per cent non-Serbs in September 1991, which then went down to half of that number; that is, less than 10 per cent in -- when you left the company.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radulj, did you, as attorney general, have any contacts from May 1992 to October 1993 with military activities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: No, I did not. Because when I left the brigade on the 15th of May, I lived in Prijedor with my family, and I was happy to have a job that didn't have to be at the front. My only task was to be on duty in front of the court building during the night. That was the duty of all the others as well. It was night guard duty. We had military rifles. And then during the day, we would be working on our regular job -- job assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May - and here we had the opportunity to hear a lot of testimony about that day and the events in Prijedor on that day - I wanted to ask you to tell us where you were that day.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I remember that morning very well, the morning of the 30th of May. I was with my wife in our apartment. The children were in the country with their grandfather and grandmother already. In the morning, I was woken up by loud shooting. I got up. My wife told me, well, that's normal, there's shooting every night, because I hadn't been in Prijedor for a while. And then I said, "I think this is something more serious." Then when it got light, I could see in front of the building that the neighbours were coming out. There were soldiers there with rifles. There was firing at the other end of the town. There was smoke. I could tell that the artillery was firing. The electricity was cut off. So even though it was a sunny day, you couldn't see anything in town because of the smoke. I was in the Pecani neighbourhood. That's where I was living.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And on that day, did you personally have any activity, requests, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: When I saw what was going on, I dressed. There's only a school in that neighbourhood. And the neighbourhood is close to the Prijedor-Novi Grad road, or actually the railway. Also, Prijedor-Novi Grad, they're parallel. Puharska is on the other side. It's a neighbourhood with a majority Muslim population. I noticed there were a number of us in uniform, without uniform, with or without weapons. I noticed that there was firing from the other side at this neighbourhood. There were also groups of people there. There was no command or any kind of leadership but they were returning fire directed at the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you join in this fighting in any way, participate in the events?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: I came to see what was going on there. This was not a line, proper classic line. There was firing, but there was also the concern not to cross over the railway line and the road so that the settlement would be attacked. I notice at one point there was a recoilless gun of the heavier weapons. The rest were infantry weapons. So one of the soldiers directed the cannon at a house which was actually the house of a friend of mine who was Muslim. And I said, "Don't fire at all. Don't fire there, especially. It's the house of a friend of mine." I told him that it was a Serb. And so he didn't. If you permit me, perhaps this is not -- has to do with all of this but it has to do with me, because that day I made a gesture. I was addressed by a certain person by the name of Salko. He was a Muslim who used to work in my company. He asked for help because his wife had gone into labour. She was about to give birth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: His daughter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the hospital was at the other end of the town. It was all unsettled. There was a lot of firing. I asked Salko, "Where is your son-in-law? Where is your daughter's husband?" And Salko said, in a weepy voice, "I don't know. He left the house two months ago." I asked him, "Is he in the Green Berets perhaps?" He said, "Possibly." I said, "Is he firing at us right now from the other side?" And he said, "That also is possible." One of the soldiers came up to me and said, "What are you talking to him for," that such and such a person. I said that is my friend. And I thought a little bit. I had an old car and I had five litres of fuel in it, and I said, "Let's go." The car was in the garage. His daughter came. He was -- she was literally holding her stomach in her hands. She was well into labour. I took a different road to avoid the conflict, and finally I reached the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me -- excuse me, can you tell me whether at the hospital, since this is a woman who was in labour but who happened to be a Muslim, did you have any problems at the hospital to have her admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I got information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. Is it the Prosecution's case that women who would report at a hospital would be refused assistance, medical assistance when giving birth? That that was always the case. It may have happened here, there, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We don't have a specific position on that. We doubt it was common, certainly. On this particular instance, the witness described it in his interview and I'm familiar with that description as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber is not familiar with any interview because it's a viva voce witness. Mr. Stojanovic, I'm waiting for the moment where we learn whether it was a girl or a boy that was born. That kind of details not really connected to what seems to be the Prosecution's case do not assist that much. The Chamber expects the Defence primarily to mount a Defence to what the Prosecution is claiming, rather than to hear from you that this witness may be a person who behaved quite well and assisted friends to get that baby born, but that is not what this case is about in general terms, and certainly those details may not be of that relevance. And if you want to put any questions, do it briefly, concretely, and not let the witness go for -- for pages to describe what seems not to be matters which are in the core of this case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was a digression, and I would just like to ask you to bear with me. Prijedor, in our indictment, remains as the town of genocide of specific intent, among other things, which would imply situations like this. If you believe that this is not relevant, about the testimony of this witness that happened, an incident that happened in the middle of the most serious events in Prijedor, I'm now going to move to something else then. Ask the witness something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your work as attorney general, did you ever have any immediate, direct contacts with Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: No, I did not. Because I didn't have any need for that. I had my own assignments which I tried to do as professionally as possible. So I had no contact, I never went there, I had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And I'm going to finish today with the following question. How did it come about that you were engaged as a military prosecutor and that you transferred to Banja Luka? In the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN RADULJ
utterances.text: A my colleague of mine, a lawyer, proposed that the -- he said that the military prosecutor's office was looking for attorneys who were also reserve officers, so I submitted a written application, which was approved, so I transferred to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radulj. Perhaps today at this point in time this is a good moment to stop, but then tomorrow we will go on with some questions about your experiences and work at the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we believe that this is a good moment to complete the examination of this witness for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although I would have one short question for you. Witness, you described your duties as attorney general, and you told us that it was your job that -- to make sure that laws and regulations were respected, especially in view of the institutions that were financed from the budget municipal organs. Would that include the respect for laws and regulations, for example, as far as the MUP was concerned, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The attorney general's role is to protect the laws and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- could you -- please. Could you please slow down. The interpreters have difficulties in following you. Could you restart your answers. You said the attorney general's role is to protect, and then please take it from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also to protect the property rights and the interests of those institutions. If we're speaking in a broader sense, and when we're talking about criminal responsibility and other forms of law violations, that was under the jurisdiction of the prosecutor's office. So that's the difference between the attorney general and the prosecutor's office, if you understand me. So just property rights and interests. When we're talking about property, land, houses, apartments, basic space. That area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only material matters. So not whether persons were -- laws were violated against persons and other citizens' rights, just property.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I'm not going to be using this document again and we'll be switching to a different topic tomorrow, I would like to tender 1D05383 now. This is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1048, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1048 is admitted. Witness, I'd like to instruct you that you shouldn't speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you gave today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 13th of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
